name: Skill Diagnostic
source: Original difficulty-ladder questions written for LSAT Trainer. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Kestrel Ridge Observatory follows a strict rule to protect the mirror of its main telescope: whenever the humidity inside the dome rises above 85 percent, the main telescope is closed for the rest of the night. The rule has no exceptions, not even for rare events such as comets or eclipses. Last Tuesday, a visiting team of students used the main telescope from dusk until dawn, and the observatory’s logs confirm that the telescope was never closed at any point that night.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: On any night when the main telescope at Kestrel Ridge is closed, the humidity inside the dome has risen above 85 percent.
The visiting students did not observe any comets or eclipses last Tuesday night.
The humidity inside the dome did not rise above 85 percent at any point last Tuesday night.
If the humidity inside the dome stays at or below 85 percent, students are permitted to use the main telescope.
The main telescope is the only instrument at Kestrel Ridge whose use is restricted by humidity.
questions.explanation: Core move: one conditional plus its contrapositive. The rule is ‘humidity above 85% → telescope closed’; since the telescope was never closed, the contrapositive gives ‘humidity never rose above 85%’ (C). The tempting trap is A, which reverses the rule into ‘closed → humidity above 85%’; it sounds like the same rule, but the telescope could be closed for other reasons (clouds, maintenance), so it does not follow. D is a reversal of a different kind (low humidity guaranteeing access), and B and E bring in matters the rule says nothing about.

questions.stimulus: At the Larchmont Dental Clinic, every patient who is scheduled for a crown fitting has already received a digital impression scan at the clinic. The clinic, in turn, performs digital impression scans only on patients who have completed a periodontal screening there. Last month several new patients joined the clinic, among them Mira Okonkwo, who has never completed a periodontal screening at Larchmont.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: If Mira Okonkwo completes a periodontal screening at Larchmont, she will receive a digital impression scan there.
Some of the patients who joined Larchmont last month have completed a periodontal screening there.
Every Larchmont patient who has received a digital impression scan there is scheduled for a crown fitting.
Mira Okonkwo cannot receive any dental treatment at Larchmont until she completes a periodontal screening.
Mira Okonkwo is not scheduled for a crown fitting at the Larchmont Dental Clinic.
questions.explanation: Core move: chaining two links and running the chain backward with the contrapositive. Crown fitting → scan → screening; Mira lacks the screening, so she has had no scan at Larchmont, and so she is not scheduled for a crown fitting (E). The most tempting trap is A, which reverses the second link: ‘only on patients who have completed a screening’ makes screening necessary for a scan, not sufficient, so finishing a screening guarantees nothing. C makes the same reversal on the first link, and D overextends the rule to all treatment.

questions.stimulus: Railway historians agree on two facts about the Varnholt Valley in the late nineteenth century. First, no branch line in the valley was built without a guaranteed freight contract. Second, a branch line was granted a guaranteed freight contract only if a mill or quarry lay within five miles of its proposed route. It follows that the Elsby branch, a Varnholt Valley branch line built in 1887, must have received a government subsidy.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: A Varnholt Valley branch line did not have a mill or quarry within five miles of its proposed route unless it received a government subsidy.
Every Varnholt Valley branch line that received a government subsidy had a mill or quarry within five miles of its proposed route.
Any Varnholt Valley branch line that lacked a guaranteed freight contract was denied a government subsidy.
Some Varnholt Valley branch lines that had guaranteed freight contracts also received government subsidies.
A Varnholt Valley branch line received a government subsidy only if it was granted a guaranteed freight contract.
questions.explanation: Core move: translating ‘no X without Y’ (built → contract), ‘only if’ (contract → mill/quarry nearby), and ‘unless’ in the answer. The chain gives Elsby → contract → mill or quarry nearby, so the gap is ‘mill or quarry nearby → subsidy’. ‘Not M unless S’ translates to ‘M → S’, which is exactly what A says. The strongest trap is E (and C, which is the same statement in contrapositive dress): both say subsidy → contract, which runs the wrong way and so cannot carry Elsby from its contract to a subsidy. B also reverses the needed link, and D’s ‘some’ is too weak to guarantee anything about Elsby.

questions.stimulus: Throughout last year, the following held for the hives of the Halloway Apiarists’ Cooperative. Every hive producing heather honey was inspected for varroa mites every month. No hive inspected every month was treated with oxalic acid during the summer. Most of the cooperative’s hives produced heather honey. Records also show that some of the cooperative’s hives were treated with oxalic acid last summer.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Some hives that were inspected for varroa mites every month did not produce heather honey.
None of the hives treated with oxalic acid last summer produced heather honey.
Some hives that did not produce heather honey were not treated with oxalic acid last summer.
At least half of the cooperative’s hives were treated with oxalic acid last summer.
Every hive in the cooperative that did not produce heather honey was treated with oxalic acid last summer.
questions.explanation: Core move: combining a conditional chain with ‘most’, then separating ‘must be false’ from ‘must be true’ and ‘could be true’. Heather → monthly inspection → no summer treatment, and most hives produced heather honey, so most hives were not treated; therefore fewer than half were treated, and D cannot be true. The top trap is B: it is attractive because it is clearly established by the chain, but that makes it must-be-true, the opposite of what the stem asks. A tempts students who reverse the first link (inspected → heather); in fact non-heather hives may also have been inspected, so A could be true, as could C and E.

questions.stimulus: Under the Torvane Arts Council’s archive policy, no recording is digitized except those whose copyright status has been cleared, and a recording’s copyright status is cleared only if the recording either has entered the public domain or is covered by a signed performer waiver. No recording made before 1960 is covered by a signed performer waiver. Admittedly, some recordings made before 1960 have been digitized. Nevertheless, the council’s 1954 recording of the Brannoch Quartet will not be digitized, since it was produced by a commercial label.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every recording that has not entered the public domain was produced by a commercial label.
No recording that has entered the public domain was produced by a commercial label.
Some recordings produced by commercial labels have not entered the public domain.
Every recording made before 1960 that was produced by a noncommercial label has been digitized.
A recording produced by a noncommercial label can have its copyright cleared only if it has entered the public domain.
questions.explanation: Core move: a multi-step chain with ‘no…except’, an either/or, and a missing link supplied in contrapositive form. Digitized → cleared → (public domain OR waiver); the Brannoch recording is pre-1960, so no waiver, so it is excluded from digitization only if it is also not in the public domain. B (public domain → not commercial) is the contrapositive of commercial → not public domain, which closes that last gap and makes the argument valid. The most tempting trap is A, which uses the same two terms but in the reverse direction (not public domain → commercial), so it says nothing about whether a commercial recording is in the public domain; C is the near-miss quantifier trap, since ‘some’ commercial recordings lacking public-domain status leaves the Brannoch recording undetermined. The concession about other pre-1960 digitized recordings is consistent with the argument: those are the public-domain ones.

questions.stimulus:
Ilse: The Morvath Glacier’s terminus retreated 40 meters last year, more than in any previous year on record. This shows that the glacier’s retreat is accelerating.

Tobias: The glacier’s retreat is not accelerating. Most of last year’s retreat came from a single calving event, when one enormous block of ice broke away at once. Apart from that event, the terminus retreated last year by about the same distance as in each of the previous ten years.
questions.stem: Ilse and Tobias disagree over whether
choices: the Morvath Glacier’s terminus retreated 40 meters last year
calving events can cause a glacier’s terminus to retreat suddenly
the Morvath Glacier’s terminus has retreated every year on record
the retreat of the Morvath Glacier is accelerating
other glaciers in the region are retreating at a steady pace
questions.explanation: Core move: finding the claim one speaker asserts and the other explicitly denies. Ilse concludes the retreat is accelerating; Tobias opens by saying it is not, so D is the point at issue. The tempting trap is A, because the 40-meter figure is the evidence the dialogue turns on, but Tobias never disputes it; he explains it away. B is asserted only by Tobias, and C and E are addressed by neither speaker.

questions.stimulus:
Renata: The Pellham Courier’s circulation has fallen every year since it began charging readers for online access. The paywall is driving readers away, so the Courier should remove it.

Gideon: That’s not right. The Harwick Ledger, a paper in the neighboring county, has never had a paywall, and its circulation has fallen just as steadily. So the Courier’s paywall cannot be responsible for any part of the Courier’s decline.
questions.stem: Gideon’s response to Renata is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats a correlation between the paywall and falling circulation as proof that the paywall caused the decline
takes for granted that, because circulation can decline without a paywall, a paywall cannot be one cause of a decline
presumes, without justification, that removing the paywall would reverse the Courier’s loss of readers
rejects the circulation figures that Renata cites without giving any reason to doubt their accuracy
relies on a comparison with a newspaper that is much larger than the Pellham Courier
questions.explanation: Core move: locating the flaw in the second speaker’s reply rather than in the first speaker’s argument. Gideon shows that circulation can fall without a paywall and concludes that the paywall contributes nothing to the Courier’s decline; a decline having one possible cause does not rule out another, which is B. The tempting trap is A: it is a fair criticism of Renata’s argument, but the stem asks about Gideon’s. C is also Renata’s presumption, D misdescribes Gideon (he accepts the figures), and nothing indicates the Ledger’s size (E).

questions.stimulus:
Anneliese: Our chess club should switch its weekly tournament to a faster time control. Most of our members now play primarily online, where fast games are the norm, so they would enjoy faster games more.

Corwin: Switching to faster games is the right decision, but your reason for it is wrong. Most of our members still play mainly over the board; only a minority play primarily online. The real reason is that our venue now closes at nine o’clock, and under the current time control many games are still unfinished when we have to leave.
questions.stem: Anneliese and Corwin are committed to agreeing that
choices: most of the club’s members play chess primarily online
members who play primarily online would enjoy faster games more than slower ones
the venue’s nine o’clock closing time leaves many tournament games unfinished
a club’s time control should match the format its members play most often
the club should switch its weekly tournament to a faster time control
questions.explanation: Core move: seeing that the speakers disagree about a premise, not the conclusion. Corwin explicitly endorses Anneliese’s conclusion (‘switching to faster games is the right decision’) while rejecting her premise, so both are committed to E. The tempting traps are claims only one speaker addresses: B is Anneliese’s supporting claim, and Corwin never says whether online players would enjoy faster games (he only disputes how many there are); C is Corwin’s alone. A is the actual point of disagreement, and D is at most an unstated principle behind Anneliese’s reasoning.

questions.stimulus:
Dr. Vasquez: The faint brightening of the star Halvren-9 recorded last spring was almost certainly caused by a passing planet acting as a gravitational lens. The brightening’s light curve was perfectly symmetrical, and lensing events always produce symmetrical light curves.

Dr. Okafor: I don’t dispute that every lensing event yields a symmetrical light curve. But the young flare stars of the Ostrava cluster regularly brighten in perfectly symmetrical pulses, and no lens is involved in any of them. Whether Halvren-9 resembles those stars, we don’t yet know.
questions.stem: Dr. Okafor responds to Dr. Vasquez’s argument by
choices: noting that the feature on which Dr. Vasquez’s conclusion rests is also displayed by events that arise in a different way
proposing that the brightening of Halvren-9 was more likely caused by stellar flaring than by gravitational lensing
challenging the claim that gravitational lensing events always produce symmetrical light curves
arguing that Dr. Vasquez’s conclusion must be false because a counterexample to it has been observed
questioning whether the brightening of Halvren-9 was measured accurately enough to support any conclusion
questions.explanation: Core move: describing how the reply works, abstractly. Vasquez treats a necessary feature of lensing (lensing → symmetry) as if it were sufficient (symmetry → lensing); Okafor grants the conditional but shows that symmetry also occurs without any lens, so the observed feature does not single out lensing (A). The strongest trap is B: Okafor mentions flare stars, but explicitly declines to say Halvren-9 is one, so he offers no rival explanation of this event. C is wrong because he expressly accepts that premise, and D is too strong, since the flare stars undermine the inference without showing the conclusion false.

questions.stimulus:
Hollis: People say competition from motor buses closed the Calder Valley Railway in 1912. Nonsense. Buses did not reach the valley until 1914, two years after the closure. The line closed because its main customer, the Dunmere slate quarry, shut in 1911, and without the slate traffic the line could not pay its way.

Priya: I don’t deny that the quarry’s closure was decisive. But your timeline is mistaken: the Fenwick company was running a regular bus service along the valley road by 1910, and the railway’s passenger receipts fell by a third between 1910 and 1912. Even so, passenger fares were never more than a small share of the railway’s income.
questions.stem: Hollis and Priya disagree over whether
choices: competition from motor buses was what caused the Calder Valley Railway to close
the loss of traffic from the Dunmere quarry was decisive in the railway’s closure
the Calder Valley had a regular motor bus service at a time when the railway was still operating
the railway’s passenger receipts fell substantially in the two years before it closed
passenger fares provided only a small portion of the railway’s income
questions.explanation: Core move: seeing past the headline issue to the narrow sub-claim actually in dispute. Hollis says buses did not reach the valley until 1914; Priya says a regular bus service ran along the valley road by 1910, while the railway (closed 1912) was still running, so they disagree about C. The most tempting trap is A, the headline issue: Hollis denies it, but Priya never commits to it, and in fact she calls the quarry decisive and the passenger income minor. B is accepted by both (Priya: ‘I don’t deny’), while D and E are claims only Priya makes; Hollis says nothing about passenger receipts or fares.

questions.stimulus: Conductor Ilse Varga has proposed that the Merriton Community Choir replace its annual oratorio performance with a program of newly commissioned works. But Varga has admitted in interviews that she finds Baroque oratorio tedious to rehearse, and she would receive a commissioning fee if one of the new works were her own. Clearly, then, the proposed change would not benefit the choir, and the board should reject it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that the choir's regular audience might prefer oratorio to unfamiliar new works
presumes, without justification, that newly commissioned works are harder to perform than oratorio
rejects a proposal on the basis of the proposer's personal preferences and possible motives rather than on the proposal's merits
treats the opinion of a single conductor as representative of the views of the entire choir
assumes that music that is tedious to rehearse must also be tedious for an audience to hear
questions.explanation: Core move: spotting an ad hominem. The argument rejects Varga's proposal only because of her tastes and a possible financial motive, which says nothing about whether the change would actually benefit the choir, so (C) is correct. The most tempting trap is (D), because treating one person's view as representative is a familiar overgeneralization; but the argument never infers the choir's views from Varga's. It dismisses her views instead. (A) names a consideration that would support the argument's conclusion, so leaving it out is not a flaw.

questions.stimulus: A survey of 400 dog owners in Calder County found that dogs walked on gravel trails at least three times a week had markedly fewer paw-pad injuries over the past year than dogs walked mainly on pavement. Veterinarian Dr. Amara Osei concludes that walking on gravel toughens a dog's paw pads and thereby protects them from injury. She therefore recommends that owners of dogs prone to paw-pad injuries switch to walking them on gravel trails.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that owners whose dogs have already suffered paw-pad injuries tend to avoid walking them on gravel
relies on a sample of dog owners that is too small to support any conclusion about dogs in general
fails to establish that gravel trails are readily accessible to every dog owner in Calder County
presumes that paw-pad injuries are the most serious health risk that dogs face
treats a recommendation that is appropriate for some dogs as though it applied to all dogs
questions.explanation: Core move: correlation vs. causation, here in the form of possible reverse causation. The survey shows only that gravel walking and fewer injuries go together. (A) points out that the cause could run the other way: if owners steer injury-prone dogs away from gravel, the same pattern would appear without gravel toughening anything. The most tempting trap is (B), since sampling flaws are common, but 400 owners is a reasonable sample, and a bigger one would not fix the real problem of interpreting the correlation. (E) fails because Osei explicitly limits her recommendation to injury-prone dogs.

questions.stimulus: At the Halloway textile mill, a bolt of linen can be certified as export grade only if it passes the mill's tensile-strength test. Last month every bolt woven on the mill's new Delmar looms passed that test, whereas nearly ten percent of the bolts woven on the older looms failed it. Plant manager Reyes concludes that all of last month's Delmar-woven bolts must have been certified as export grade, and that bolts from the older looms account for every bolt denied certification last month.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: treats one month's production as representative of the looms' performance over a longer period
fails to consider that some bolts woven on the older looms may have been certified as export grade
presumes that the Delmar looms produced more bolts last month than the older looms did
compares two kinds of looms that may differ in ways other than their test results
treats passing the tensile-strength test as though it ensured certification rather than merely being required for it
questions.explanation: Core move: necessary vs. sufficient. The 'only if' premise makes passing the tensile test a requirement for certification, yet Reyes concludes that every bolt that passed was certified. That treats a necessary condition as a sufficient one, as (E) says. The most tempting trap is (A), a sampling-style flaw. It fails because both of Reyes's conclusions concern last month only, so the argument never generalizes beyond the month it sampled. (B) describes something the argument never denies: Reyes claims that every denied bolt came from the older looms, not that no older-loom bolt was certified.

questions.stimulus: Some members of the Fenwick Cooperative Bank charge that it has been shortchanging the small farmers it was founded to serve. Yet five years ago agricultural loans made up 30 percent of the money the cooperative lent, and this year they make up 34 percent. Admittedly, the cooperative has closed two rural branch offices during that period, and some farmers now travel farther to apply for loans. Nevertheless, since agriculture commands a larger share of the cooperative's lending than it did five years ago, farmers must be receiving more loan money from the cooperative now than they were then.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that the farmers who must now travel farther to apply for loans have not stopped applying altogether
takes for granted that an increase in the proportion of a total devoted to one purpose guarantees an increase in the amount devoted to that purpose
presumes without justification that the members who made the charge are themselves small farmers
bases a conclusion about a trend on a comparison of only two years, ignoring the years in between
attacks the motives of the members who made the charge rather than addressing the charge itself
questions.explanation: Core move: percentage vs. absolute number, stated abstractly. Agriculture's share rose from 30 to 34 percent, but if the cooperative's total lending shrank enough, 34 percent of the new total could be less money than 30 percent of the old. The argument takes for granted that a larger share means a larger amount, as (B) says. The strongest trap is (A), which plays off the concession; but any farmers who stopped applying are already reflected in the 34 percent figure, so the argument does not need to assume they kept applying. (D) is tempting as a sampling complaint, but the conclusion compares only now with five years ago, so the intervening years do not matter.

questions.stimulus: The Talvessa wetland's mosquitoes lay their eggs only on open water. The Orrin-3 satellite photographs the wetland at a resolution that reveals any patch of open water larger than four square meters, and researchers found no open water in any of its images of the wetland's northern basin from the past dry season. Granted, the satellite passes over the basin only once every nine days. But the basin's clay soils are such that any standing water there would persist for weeks. So the northern basin held no open water during the dry season, and it therefore could not have been a mosquito breeding site that season.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that it
choices: overlooks the possibility that standing water formed and disappeared between two of the satellite's passes over the basin
takes for granted that the mosquitoes could not have laid their eggs anywhere other than on open water
infers that a characteristic of one region of the wetland must hold for the wetland as a whole
treats the failure to detect any instance of something above a certain size as showing that no instance of it, of any size, was present
confuses a reason for believing that the basin was dry with a cause of the basin's being dry
questions.explanation: Core move: absence of evidence treated as evidence of absence, in a subtle form. The satellite registers only patches of open water larger than four square meters, so finding none shows only that no large patches existed. The argument concludes that there was no open water at all, though mosquitoes could breed in small pools, which is the gap (D) describes. (A) is the most tempting trap because it names a real-sounding gap in the satellite record, but the argument closes it: water in the basin would persist for weeks, longer than the nine days between passes. (B) is also a real-sounding flaw, but the first premise rules it out, and (C) fails because the conclusion concerns only the northern basin, not the wetland as a whole.

questions.stimulus: Honeybees from the rooftop hives in the city of Dunmore gather nectar mainly in the city's public gardens. This spring, the city replaced most of the flowering shrubs in those gardens with ornamental grasses, which provide bees with no nectar at all. Beekeepers in Dunmore therefore predict that their rooftop hives will produce less honey this year than they did last year.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Ornamental grasses are less attractive to honeybees than flowering shrubs are.
The flowering shrubs that were removed had supplied some of the nectar from which the rooftop hives' bees made honey.
Honeybees cannot make honey from the nectar of any plants other than flowering shrubs.
Dunmore's rooftop hives produced more honey last year than any other hives in the region.
The city will not replant flowering shrubs in its public gardens at any point this year.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the obvious bridge between premise and conclusion. The prediction links removing the shrubs to less honey, which works only if those shrubs actually supplied nectar the bees used. Negate (B), so that the shrubs supplied none of that nectar, and their removal gives no reason to expect less honey. The tempting trap is (C): it would strengthen the argument, but it is far too strong, since the bees could also use nectar from flower beds or other plants and the prediction would still hold. (E) is not required either, because honey production could fall even if some shrubs were replanted late in the year.

questions.stimulus: The Kessler Ridge trail crew plans to reroute a badly eroded section of trail onto a gentler slope and close the old section to hikers. The crew leader argues that the reroute will reduce the total time the crew spends each year on erosion repair along that part of the ridge, since trails on gentle slopes erode far more slowly than trails on steep ones.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Most hikers prefer walking on trails with gentle slopes to walking on trails with steep ones.
Trails on gentle slopes never require any erosion repair at all.
The reroute can be completed within a single working season.
After the reroute, the crew will not need to keep repairing the old section as often as it does now.
Erosion is the most time-consuming problem the crew deals with anywhere on Kessler Ridge.
questions.explanation: Core move: a defender assumption that blocks one way the plan could fail. The conclusion concerns total repair time along that part of the ridge, so if the crew still had to repair the closed old section as often as it does now (the negation of D), adding even slow-eroding new trail would not reduce the total. The tempting trap is (B), which would guarantee that the new section needs no repair but is far stronger than required; the argument needs only that the new section erodes more slowly, as the premise says. (E) is irrelevant because the conclusion concerns erosion repair on this section, not erosion's rank among the crew's problems.

questions.stimulus: The Barrow Vale dye works currently rinses each batch of dyed wool in three successive fills of fresh water. A new recirculating system filters and reuses rinse water, so each batch needs only a single fill of fresh water. The system's filtration units must be flushed with fresh water once a week, but the works' manager nonetheless concludes that switching to the new system will reduce the dye works' total consumption of fresh water.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The fresh water needed each week to flush the filtration units is less than the fresh water the new system saves on rinsing over the same week.
The new system rinses wool at least as thoroughly as the current three-fill method does.
Flushing the filtration units requires less fresh water than a single rinse of one batch of wool does.
A single fill of fresh water in the new system holds no more water than one fill under the current method.
Other dye works that have adopted recirculating systems have reported lower water bills.
questions.explanation: Core move: a 'does not completely offset' assumption. The new system saves two fills per batch but adds a weekly flush, so a net reduction requires that the flush not use up or exceed the savings, which is what (A) states. Negate it and switching saves nothing. The most tempting trap is (C), which sounds like a sensible cost comparison but is too strong: the flush happens once a week while savings accrue on every batch, so it could use more water than one rinse and the system would still come out ahead. (D) is likewise unnecessary, since even a somewhat larger single fill could use less than three ordinary ones, and (B) concerns rinse quality, which the argument about water use never relies on.

questions.stimulus: Every licensed beekeeper in the city of Harlow must register each hive he or she keeps, and the city's registry currently lists 640 hives. Yet a survey of Harlow's rooftops conducted last month counted 910 hives. Admittedly, the registry also includes hives kept in backyards and community gardens, not just on rooftops, but that only widens the gap between the registry and the survey. So the city's apiary inspector is right to conclude that a substantial number of Harlow's hives are being kept by people who hold no beekeeping license.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: The rooftop survey did not count any single hive more than once.
No licensed beekeeper in Harlow keeps a hive that he or she has failed to register.
The rooftop survey located every hive that is kept on a rooftop in Harlow.
Most of the hives kept in backyards and community gardens in Harlow are registered.
Licensed beekeepers who have failed to register some of their hives do not account for nearly all of Harlow's unregistered hives.
questions.explanation: Core move: a minimal 'not nearly all' defender assumption. The gap between 910 surveyed hives and 640 registered ones could be explained by licensed beekeepers who simply neglected to register some hives. The conclusion about unlicensed keepers requires that such hives not account for nearly all of the gap, which (E) states; negate it and the conclusion collapses. (B) is the strongest trap: it would make the argument airtight, but it is too strong, since a few licensed keepers with an unregistered hive or two would leave the conclusion intact. (A) and (C) are also too strong: a few double-counted hives would not undermine the conclusion, and a survey that missed hives would only make the unregistered count larger.

questions.stimulus: Satellite images of the Sedra River delta show that the area covered by mangrove forest was 18 percent smaller in 2025 than in 2015. Admittedly, shrimp farming expanded rapidly in the delta during that decade, and conservation groups have blamed the shrimp ponds for the loss. But the 2015 images show that every pond now in the delta occupies land that was bare mudflat at that time, so the ponds displaced no mangroves. The bulk of the loss, then, must be due to the rising sea, which has been submerging the delta's seaward fringe.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Rising sea level and shrimp farming are the only developments that could have reduced the delta's mangrove area over the decade.
None of the measured decline in mangrove area reflects differences in the way the 2015 and 2025 images were recorded or classified.
Differences in the way the 2015 and 2025 images were recorded or classified do not account for most of the measured decline in mangrove area.
No mangroves had been cleared, at any time before 2015, from the land that the shrimp ponds now occupy.
The rising sea submerged more of the delta between 2015 and 2025 than in any previous decade.
questions.explanation: Core move: a defender assumption that rules out an alternative the stimulus never raises, namely that the measured loss is partly an artifact of measurement. The argument eliminates the shrimp ponds and concludes that the sea accounts for the bulk of the loss. If differences in how the two sets of images were recorded or classified produced most of the measured decline (the negation of C), most of that 'loss' would not be due to the sea at all. (A) is the most tempting trap: together with the premises it would prove the conclusion, but it is not required, because other factors could exist as long as they are minor. (B) differs from (C) by one quantifier and is too strong, since a small measurement artifact would leave the 'bulk' conclusion untouched, and (D) concerns clearing before 2015, which is irrelevant to a decline measured from 2015 onward.

questions.stimulus: The Lindell Veterinary Board approves a vaccine only after reviewing the results of a two-year safety trial, and it approves no vaccine that has failed such a trial. Felinor, a new vaccine against feline respiratory disease that its manufacturer plans to market to owners of young cats, received the board's approval last spring. Therefore, Felinor is safe to give to kittens.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Felinor is safe to give to adult cats.
Any vaccine that is safe to give to kittens has passed a two-year safety trial.
The Lindell Veterinary Board approves only vaccines intended for cats.
Any vaccine that has passed a two-year safety trial is safe to give to kittens.
Most vaccines that have passed a two-year safety trial are safe to give to kittens.
questions.explanation: Core move: supply the single missing link in a two-step chain. The premises establish that Felinor passed a two-year safety trial; the conclusion needs 'passed the trial → safe for kittens,' which is exactly (D). The tempting trap is (B), which uses the same two terms but reverses the conditional: knowing that every kitten-safe vaccine passed a trial says nothing about whether a vaccine that passed one is kitten-safe. (E) has the right direction but is too weak, since 'most' leaves room for Felinor to be an exception.

questions.stimulus: The Pinecrest Trail Association will rebuild the Miller Creek footbridge this year only if it receives a state recreation grant, and the state awards such grants only to applicants that submit a completed environmental review. At its last meeting, the association's board voted not to hire a wetland surveyor this year. So the Miller Creek footbridge will not be rebuilt this year.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: If the association hires a wetland surveyor, it will be able to submit a completed environmental review.
The association cannot submit a completed environmental review this year unless it hires a wetland surveyor.
A state recreation grant is the association's only possible source of funds for rebuilding the footbridge.
Any applicant that submits a completed environmental review will receive a state recreation grant.
The board would have voted to hire a wetland surveyor if the association had more funds.
questions.explanation: Core move: link a negated premise to a negated conclusion. The premises give 'rebuild → grant → completed review'; to get 'not rebuilt' from 'no surveyor hired,' we need 'completed review → surveyor hired.' Then no surveyor means no review, no grant, and no bridge, and (B) supplies that link. The tempting trap is (A), which reverses it: a surveyor being enough for a review tells us nothing about what happens without one. (C) restates what the 'only if' premise already establishes, and (D) reverses the grant condition.

questions.stimulus: Every piece on the Halden Choir's spring program is either sung a cappella or accompanied by organ, and no piece sung a cappella requires the tenors to rehearse with the accompanist. The motet Lumen Aeternum, which is on the spring program, does require the tenors to rehearse with the accompanist. It follows that Lumen Aeternum will not be performed at the choir's chapel concert.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every piece on the spring program that is sung a cappella will be performed at the chapel concert.
Some pieces on the spring program that are accompanied by organ will not be performed at the chapel concert.
Every piece on the spring program that requires the tenors to rehearse with the accompanist is accompanied by organ.
None of the pieces performed at the chapel concert will require the sopranos to rehearse with the accompanist.
Every piece on the spring program that will be performed at the chapel concert is sung a cappella.
questions.explanation: Core move: a conditional whose contrapositive finishes the chain. Lumen Aeternum requires the tenors to rehearse with the accompanist, so by the contrapositive of the second premise it is not sung a cappella. (E) says every chapel piece is sung a cappella, and its contrapositive (any piece not sung a cappella is not performed at the chapel) yields the conclusion. The main competitor is (A), which uses the same terms in the reverse direction: knowing that a cappella pieces will be performed at the chapel says nothing about pieces that are not sung a cappella. (C) only restates what the premises already imply and never mentions the chapel, and (B) is too weak because 'some' organ pieces need not include Lumen Aeternum.

questions.stimulus: At the Brindle Cooperative Bank, no one may vote in board elections without holding at least one share. Holding a share does not by itself guarantee a dividend, however: every shareholding member is entitled to the annual dividend unless that member has a loan in default with the cooperative. Okonkwo voted in this year's board election. It follows that Okonkwo is entitled to this year's annual dividend.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every member who is entitled to the annual dividend is eligible to vote in board elections.
Okonkwo holds at least one share in the cooperative.
No member who has a loan in default with the cooperative is permitted to vote in board elections.
Any member who holds more than one share has no loan in default with the cooperative.
Any member who is not permitted to vote in board elections has a loan in default with the cooperative.
questions.explanation: Core move: a 'no X is Y' link whose contrapositive closes a chain built on 'unless.' Voting shows that Okonkwo holds a share, and a shareholder gets the dividend unless he has a loan in default, so the conclusion needs Okonkwo to have no defaulted loan. (C) supplies this indirectly: no one with a defaulted loan may vote, and Okonkwo voted, so he has no defaulted loan. (E) is the strongest trap, the reversed conditional ('not permitted to vote → default'), which says nothing about members who did vote. (B) is a necessary-but-not-sufficient bridge that already follows from the premises and leaves the default question open, and (D) fails because Okonkwo may hold only one share.

questions.stimulus: None of the translations of Vessk poetry that Ilmar Press published this year is eligible for the Corwen Prize. After all, the prize's rules exclude any translation made from a relay text, that is, from an existing translation in a third language. And every translation Ilmar published this year was made from a relay text unless its translator holds a state certificate in the source language. Admittedly, Ilmar employs several certified translators, so some of its translations this year may well be eligible; but that does not alter the case of its Vessk poetry.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the conclusion of the argument to be properly drawn?
choices: No translator who holds a state certificate in Vessk translated any of the Vessk poetry that Ilmar Press published this year.
Most of the Vessk poetry that Ilmar Press published this year was translated by people who hold no state certificate in Vessk.
Every translation that Ilmar Press published this year by a certified translator was made directly from its source language.
Any translation made directly from its source language rather than from a relay text is eligible for the Corwen Prize.
Every translator Ilmar Press employed this year who lacks a state certificate in the source language worked from a relay text.
questions.explanation: Core move: a 'no X is Y' statement that, through an 'unless' premise, completes a chain to a conclusion stated first. The premises say that any Ilmar translation this year whose translator lacks a certificate in the source language was made from a relay text, and relay translations are ineligible. So the conclusion follows if no Vessk-certified translator did any of Ilmar's Vessk poetry, as (A) says. (B) is the near-miss: it differs by one quantifier, and 'most' leaves room for some Vessk poetry by certified translators, which could be eligible. (C) is tempting because it reads 'unless' as a biconditional and echoes the concession, but even if certified translators always work directly from the source, nothing yet shows that none of the Vessk poetry was done by one. (D) reverses the eligibility rule, and (E) merely restates the premise about uncertified translators.

questions.stimulus: Three years ago, the town of Pell replaced the asphalt in all of its public parking lots with permeable paving, which allows rainwater to pass through it into the soil below. Since then, the peak flow of Marrow Creek, which drains the town, has been roughly 20 percent lower after heavy storms than it was before the change. Hydrologists in Pell conclude that the new paving is responsible for the reduction in the creek's storm peaks.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Permeable paving is considerably more expensive to install than conventional asphalt.
The firm that installed Pell's permeable paving has completed similar projects in many other towns.
In several other towns that replaced asphalt lots with permeable paving, storm peaks in the local creeks dropped by similar amounts afterward.
Pell's residents voted by a wide margin in favor of replacing the asphalt lots.
Storms in the Marrow Creek watershed over the past three years have been, on average, less intense than those of the preceding decade.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the choice that directly supports the causal conclusion by showing the same cause produces the same effect elsewhere. C does exactly that: repeated cases in which permeable paving was followed by similar drops in storm peaks make it more likely that the paving, not chance, explains Pell's drop. The tempting trap is B, which also mentions other towns, but it tells us only that the installer was busy, not what happened to any creek. E is the wrong-direction trap: gentler storms are an alternative explanation for lower peaks, so it weakens the argument.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Fernhollow Press redesigned its long-running early-reader series, switching to larger type and adding an illustration to every page. In the twelve months after the redesigned books appeared, sales of the series rose by 30 percent over the previous twelve months. Fernhollow's editors conclude that the redesign made the series more appealing to young readers and the parents who buy books for them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Sales of other publishers' early-reader series, none of which changed their designs, stayed roughly flat over the same twelve months.
Fernhollow also substantially increased its advertising for the series last year.
Printing a book with an illustration on every page costs Fernhollow more than its previous format did.
Reading specialists disagree about whether frequent illustrations help or hinder beginning readers in learning to decode words.
Fernhollow plans to apply the same redesign to its chapter-book series next year.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a before-and-after causal claim by ruling out an alternative cause. A shows the whole early-reader market did not grow, so the 30 percent rise cannot be explained by a general boom and is more plausibly due to Fernhollow's change. The most tempting trap is D, because it is about the redesign's features, but the conclusion is about appeal to buyers, not about whether the illustrations teach reading well; a disagreement among specialists bears on neither. B is a weakener, offering advertising as a rival cause.

questions.stimulus: Volunteers at the Carrow Point banding station caught and banded 2,400 migrating warblers this autumn, and only 9 percent of them were first-year birds hatched that summer. A decade ago, first-year birds made up about 25 percent of the warblers banded at the station each autumn. The station's director concludes that the breeding success of the warbler populations that migrate past Carrow Point has declined sharply over the past decade.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Adult warblers are better than first-year warblers at avoiding the mist nets used at banding stations.
Many of the warblers banded at Carrow Point this autumn were later recaptured at stations farther south.
The number of volunteers working at the station has roughly doubled over the past decade.
First-year warblers are generally lighter than adults when they pass Carrow Point.
Throughout the past decade, the station has operated its nets at the same locations and during the same weeks each autumn.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen by confirming that the samples being compared are comparable, so the change in the numbers reflects a change in the birds rather than in the sampling. E rules out the possibility that moved nets or shifted dates caught a different mix of ages this year than a decade ago. The tempting trap is A, which is about sampling bias and so feels on point; but a bias that is the same every year affects both figures alike and cannot explain why the share of young birds fell. C mentions a change at the station, but more volunteers banding the same nets would not change the age mix.

questions.stimulus: At Halvard Clinic, patients whose knee replacements were done with the Corin technique, which preserves a thigh-muscle tendon that the standard technique cuts, walked unassisted an average of nine days sooner than patients given the standard technique. Admittedly, surgeons chose which technique to use, and they tended to use the Corin technique on younger patients. But even among patients under sixty, those given the Corin technique walked unassisted sooner. So the faster recovery is attributable to the preservation of the tendon.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Younger patients generally regain mobility after knee replacement faster than older patients do.
When the tendon is cut, the thigh muscle it anchors cannot generate enough force to stabilize the knee during walking until the tendon has reattached, which takes about a week.
The Corin technique also requires a somewhat smaller incision than the standard technique does.
Most surgeons who have tried the Corin technique now prefer it to the standard technique.
Patients under sixty make up only a small fraction of the clinic's knee-replacement patients.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen by supplying the mechanism that links the specific feature named in the conclusion (the tendon) to the effect. The premises at most show the Corin technique helps; B explains how cutting the tendon would delay walking by about the observed amount, which makes the tendon, rather than some other feature of the technique, the likely cause. The strongest trap is A: it supports the concession about age, which the argument already answered with the under-sixty comparison, so it adds nothing to the conclusion and if anything highlights a confound. D supports a different conclusion (that the technique is better overall), and C offers a rival feature, so it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Brenford restaurants in the western districts, now inspected by unannounced teams, averaged 4.1 recorded violations per inspection, while those in the eastern districts, still inspected on a schedule announced a week ahead, averaged 2.3. Some council members take this as evidence that western restaurants are less sanitary. Granted, the western districts contain more of the city's older buildings. But scheduled inspections are known to understate violations, since restaurants can prepare for them. So the council members' inference is unwarranted, and if unannounced inspections were extended to the east, recorded violations there would likely approach the western level.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: Restaurants that learn of an inspection a week in advance typically use that time to correct problems an inspector would otherwise cite.
Unannounced inspections are more effective than scheduled ones at reducing the incidence of foodborne illness.
Older restaurant buildings are more difficult to keep free of pests than newer ones are.
Four years ago, before unannounced inspections began, western and eastern restaurants averaged nearly identical numbers of recorded violations per scheduled inspection.
Several eastern-district restaurants have voluntarily requested unannounced inspections in order to reassure customers.
questions.explanation: Core move: strengthen a comparison by establishing a baseline, an answer that looks like irrelevant history on first read. D shows that when both halves of the city were measured the same way, they looked the same; so the current gap appeared with the change in method, which supports both that the gap is not about sanitation (despite the older buildings) and that eastern numbers would rise under the new method. The main trap is A: it feels like strong support, but it only restates a premise the argument already gives (scheduled inspections understate violations because restaurants prepare), and it says nothing about how large the understatement is relative to the gap. B supports a different conclusion, a policy recommendation the author never makes, and C strengthens the conceded alternative, so it weakens.

questions.stimulus: Since the Tallow Ridge wind farm began operating two years ago, crews inspecting the ground beneath its forty turbines have found dozens of dead bats each late summer, far more than they find in any other season. The ridge lies on a known migration route for several bat species. Local conservationists conclude that the turbines' spinning blades are killing bats that fly over the ridge during their seasonal migration.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Many bat species in the region migrate during late summer and early autumn.
Examinations show that most of the dead bats found beneath the turbines died of a fungal disease that has recently spread through the region's bat colonies.
Wind turbines generate electricity without producing greenhouse gas emissions.
The turbines at Tallow Ridge are taller than those at most other wind farms in the region.
Dead bats have also been found beneath the turbines of several other wind farms.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a causal conclusion by giving a different cause for the observed effect. If most of the bats died of disease, the presence of carcasses under the turbines no longer shows the blades killed them. The tempting trap is E, because it is about dead bats at wind farms and so feels relevant; but it is consistent with turbines killing bats and, if anything, strengthens the conclusion. A merely supports the premise that bats pass by during migration.

questions.stimulus: When the Ashgrove Public Library eliminated overdue fines last year, the number of books returned late fell by 15 percent compared with the year before, even though the library lent out about the same number of books in both years. The library's director argues that fines had been discouraging timely returns, because borrowers who owed fines avoided the library, and that eliminating fines is what produced the decline in late returns.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Eliminating fines cost the library a significant portion of its annual revenue.
Many borrowers surveyed last year said they had avoided the library in the past while they owed fines.
The 15 percent figure was compiled by library staff rather than by outside auditors.
At the same time it eliminated fines, the library began sending borrowers automated reminders a few days before their books were due.
Some borrowers who returned books late last year had also returned books late in earlier years.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a before-and-after argument by identifying a simultaneous change that could explain the result. Due-date reminders are an independent reason late returns would fall, so the decline no longer points to the fine policy. The tempting traps are A, which attacks the policy on a ground (revenue) the director never claims anything about, and C, which tries to cast doubt on the 15 percent figure, a premise we must accept as given. B actually strengthens the director's proposed mechanism.

questions.stimulus: An analysis of 3,000 listings on Drivemart, an online used-car marketplace, found that cars advertised with a complete set of service records sold for 12 percent more, on average, than cars of the same make, model, age, and mileage advertised without them. The analysts conclude that a seller who assembles complete service records before listing a car can expect to raise its sale price by about 12 percent.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Owners who keep complete service records also tend to maintain their cars more carefully, so their cars are typically in better mechanical condition than comparable cars without records.
Cars sold through Drivemart typically fetch slightly higher prices than similar cars sold through dealerships.
Many buyers surveyed said that service records gave them confidence that a car had been well maintained.
Assembling a complete set of service records can take a seller many hours of work.
Some of the cars listed with complete service records had been in minor accidents.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken a correlation-to-causation leap by showing the supposed cause is a marker for a hidden factor. If cars with records are simply better cars, the 12 percent premium reflects condition, and a seller who merely gathers paperwork for an ordinary car would not capture it. The most tempting trap is D, which attacks whether assembling records is worthwhile, a claim the analysts never make; their claim is only about the price increase. B is tempting as a representativeness worry, but a different price level across venues says nothing about the size of the percentage premium, and C strengthens.

questions.stimulus: Marine biologists transplanted fragments of staghorn coral bred at the Ilsa Bay nursery onto a degraded section of the Varro Reef. Two years later, a marine heat wave struck; 70 percent of the transplanted fragments survived it, compared with 30 percent of the wild staghorn on an adjacent section. Admittedly, a few transplants were lost to storms before the heat wave, but these were excluded from the count. The result shows, the biologists say, that the nursery's breeding program has produced staghorn substantially more resistant to heat stress than wild staghorn.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Wild staghorn on other sections of the Varro Reef suffered losses in the heat wave similar to those on the adjacent section.
The transplanted fragments grew more slowly during their two years on the reef than wild staghorn on the adjacent section did.
Bleached but still-living staghorn can be hard to distinguish from dead coral, so divers' survival counts after heat waves are sometimes inaccurate.
The nursery's fragments were bred from parent colonies collected on the Varro Reef itself.

Before transplanting, the nursery grows all fragments in tanks whose temperature is gradually raised, a treatment known to boost any coral's heat tolerance for several years regardless of its parentage.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken by separating the factor the conclusion credits (breeding) from another feature of the same treatment (tank conditioning). The data show nursery corals survived better, but E supplies a non-genetic reason they would, so the result no longer shows the breeding program produced more heat-resistant corals. Two traps are strong: B attacks a claim the biologists never make (that the corals are better overall), and C tries to weaken the survival data, which are given as premises; besides, a counting difficulty applies to both groups and gives no reason to think the gap is exaggerated. A strengthens by showing the comparison group was typical.

questions.stimulus: Since the Marlow Opera House began selling $20 rush tickets to patrons under thirty, 18 percent of its ticket buyers have been under thirty, compared with 7 percent at the Venn Opera, which offers no such discount. Venn's board had long believed that opera simply does not appeal to young adults. It now concludes that it was wrong: young adults will attend opera when it is affordable. Hence, the board reasons, a rush-ticket program at Venn would substantially increase the share of its ticket buyers who are under thirty.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Adults under thirty in Venn's city, when surveyed, most often cite ticket prices as their reason for not attending opera.
Some of Marlow's ticket buyers under thirty pay full price rather than buying rush tickets.
In the season before Marlow introduced rush tickets, 16 percent of its ticket buyers were already under thirty.
Marlow sells its rush tickets for less than it costs to fill each seat for a performance.
Venn's board originally adopted its view of young audiences on the basis of a survey conducted more than a decade ago.
questions.explanation: Core move: weaken by undermining the comparison through its base rate. The argument treats the 18-versus-7 gap as the effect of rush tickets, but C shows Marlow's young share was already 16 percent before the program, so nearly all of the gap predates the discount and gives little reason to expect a program to transform Venn's numbers. The sneakiest trap is B, which hinges on a quantifier: if most young Marlow buyers paid full price, the discount would look irrelevant, but some paying full price is fully compatible with the program driving attendance. A strengthens, D attacks the program's finances (a claim never made), and E attacks the board's old belief, which the board has already abandoned.

questions.stimulus: The turbines at the Gorran Flats wind farm generate the most electricity in winter, when winds in the area are strongest, and the least in summer, when calm days are common. The farm sells all of its output to the regional grid and has no other significant source of income. Yet the wind farm's revenue from selling electricity to the regional grid is consistently highest in summer.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Winds at Gorran Flats are stronger in every season than at most other wind farms in the region.
The farm's turbines need more frequent maintenance in winter, when ice forms on their blades.
Summer days are considerably longer than winter days at Gorran Flats's latitude.
The price the regional grid pays for each unit of electricity is several times higher in summer, when demand for air-conditioning peaks, than in winter.
Several new wind farms in the region began selling electricity to the grid last year.
questions.explanation: Core move: reconcile two facts by finding the missing variable that links them; here revenue depends on price as well as quantity. D shows that a smaller summer output sells at a much higher price, so summer revenue can exceed winter revenue. The tempting trap is B, which explains higher winter costs, but costs do not affect revenue, and the stimulus already says winter output is highest. C is irrelevant because turbines run on wind, not daylight.

questions.stimulus: Bookstore sales of a picture book typically triple in the year after it wins the Brambling Medal, a prize awarded annually to one picture book and announced with considerable publicity. The county's libraries, like most, keep at least one copy of each winner on their shelves. Yet in Calder County's public libraries, medal-winning picture books are checked out less often in the year after winning than in the year before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Bookstores prominently display and promote medal winners in the months after the award is announced.
Many parents who learn that a picture book has won the medal buy a copy for their own household rather than borrowing it from a library.
The committee that selects the Brambling Medal winner is made up largely of children's librarians.
Picture books are checked out from Calder County's libraries more often than any other kind of children's book.
Some books that have won the Brambling Medal were already bestsellers before receiving it.
questions.explanation: Core move: find the one fact that connects the two trends, so that the rise in one actually produces the fall in the other. If families who once borrowed medal winners now buy them, the award drives sales up and library checkouts down simultaneously. The tempting trap is A: it explains the jump in bookstore sales but leaves the library decline unexplained. E concerns only a few books and explains neither trend.

questions.stimulus: At Westmere Hospital last year, patients whose hip fractures were surgically repaired within 24 hours of admission had a higher rate of complications than patients whose surgery took place more than 48 hours after admission, even after the hospital accounted for differences in the patients' ages. Yet large studies consistently find that, for hip-fracture patients generally, delaying surgery increases the risk of complications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Complications associated with delayed surgery include blood clots and pneumonia, both of which can result from prolonged bed rest.
Westmere's surgeons perform more hip-fracture repairs each year than surgeons at most comparable hospitals do.
Most of the large studies of surgical timing were conducted at hospitals considerably larger than Westmere.
Hip fractures are much more common among elderly people than among younger people.
Westmere operates immediately mainly on patients with severe, displaced fractures, while patients with simple, stable fractures are scheduled later as operating rooms become free.
questions.explanation: Core move: resolve a conflict between a local result and a general finding by showing the local comparison groups differ. If Westmere's early-surgery group is made up of the hardest cases, it can have more complications even though, for any given patient, delay is harmful, so both facts stand. The most tempting trap is A, which explains why delay is generally harmful but does nothing to explain Westmere's reverse pattern. C is tempting because it hints Westmere is different, but hospital size alone gives no reason early surgery would go worse there.

questions.stimulus: Over the past decade, live coral cover on the Selka Atoll's reefs has increased by about a third, reversing earlier losses. Over the same period, annual surveys have recorded a steady decline in the number of reef-fish species present at the atoll, and the decline has been as steep among species that no fishery targets as among commercially caught species. Since reef fish depend on corals for food and shelter, marine ecologists had expected the coral's recovery to bring a recovery in fish diversity.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The coral recovery has consisted almost entirely of a single fast-growing plating species, which has overgrown the branching corals whose complex shapes shelter many reef-fish species.
Commercial fishing around the atoll has intensified considerably over the past decade.
Since a ban on boat anchoring took effect ten years ago, damaged coral on the atoll has been steadily regrowing.
Many reef-fish species at the atoll feed mainly on algae rather than on coral itself.
The fish species that have disappeared from the atoll's surveys are still found on reefs elsewhere in the region.
questions.explanation: Core move: choose the answer that explains both facts at once and fits every detail of the stimulus, while traps explain only one side. A explains why coral cover rose (a fast-growing species spread) and why fish diversity fell (that spread destroyed the complex habitat many species need). B is the strongest trap, a natural explanation for fewer fish, but the stimulus already rules it out by noting that untargeted species declined just as steeply. C explains only the coral increase, and D at most weakens the ecologists' expectation without explaining why diversity actually declined.

questions.stimulus: Last season the Halvorsen Opera raised the price of every seat by about a quarter, expecting to sell fewer tickets but to earn more overall. Instead, the number of tickets it sold rose by 10 percent. Its audience surveys showed no change in the age or income of its patrons. Over the same season, the city's two other opera companies kept their prices unchanged, and both sold fewer tickets than the season before.
questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above EXCEPT:
choices: Many operagoers in the city treat a higher ticket price as a sign of a more lavish production, and Halvorsen's prices are now the highest in the city.
Halvorsen's season included several of the most popular works in the operatic repertory, whereas its competitors staged mostly unfamiliar operas.
Even before Halvorsen raised its prices, its tickets cost more than comparable seats at either of the other companies.
A celebrated tenor who had previously sung mainly with one of the other companies joined Halvorsen's company last season.
Halvorsen reopened last season in a renovated hall whose improved sightlines and acoustics drew widespread favorable press coverage.
questions.explanation: Core move: in an EXCEPT explain question, eliminate the four choices that resolve the discrepancy and find the one that only seems to. C sounds like an explanation because it is about relative price, but it only shows Halvorsen became even more expensive relative to rivals, which deepens the puzzle of why its sales rose while theirs fell. The most tempting trap is A, which looks odd enough to pick as the EXCEPT, but if patrons read high prices as a signal of quality, the price increase itself could draw buyers, so it does explain. B, D, and E each give patrons a reason to shift from the rivals to Halvorsen, explaining both Halvorsen's gain and the rivals' losses.

questions.stimulus: The water level in Brinley Reservoir fell sharply over the course of this summer, reaching its lowest point in more than twenty years. The reservoir is fed by streams draining the surrounding hills. The regional water authority attributes the drop to increased household water use by the residents of Brinley, a fast-growing town that draws all of its water from the reservoir.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether rainfall in the area that drains into Brinley Reservoir was much lower this summer than in previous summers
Whether most Brinley residents would support restrictions on lawn watering
When Brinley Reservoir was originally constructed
Whether other towns in the region also draw their water from reservoirs
Whether Brinley's population is expected to keep growing next year
questions.explanation: Core move: an evaluate question asks for the information whose answer would change how strong the argument is, and the obvious candidate is a rival cause. If rainfall was unusually low, drought could explain the drop and the argument weakens; if rainfall was normal, the household-use explanation gains ground. The tempting trap is E, since it concerns the town's growth, but future growth says nothing about what caused this summer's drop. B concerns a possible remedy, not the cause.

questions.stimulus: Since Corvel City began requiring restaurants to post their latest inspection grades in their front windows, reported cases of foodborne illness traced to restaurants have dropped by 20 percent compared with the year before the rule took effect. The number of restaurants in the city has stayed roughly constant. A city official argues that the posting requirement has motivated restaurants to improve their hygiene practices.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether restaurants with high posted grades charge higher prices than those with low grades
Whether some other cities post restaurant inspection grades online rather than in windows
Whether restaurants' average inspection scores have risen since the posting requirement took effect
Whether foodborne illness is generally more common in summer than in winter
Whether the posted grade signs are printed in more than one language
questions.explanation: Core move: test the official's mechanism directly. If inspection scores rose, there is independent evidence that hygiene improved, supporting the argument; if scores stayed flat, the drop in illness likely has some other cause, weakening it. The tempting trap is B, which is about grade posting, but how other cities publish grades says nothing about what happened in Corvel. D is tempting as a possible confound, but a seasonal pattern recurs every year and so cannot explain a year-over-year decline.

questions.stimulus: Last year, Hartwell Motors, a used-car dealership, stopped negotiating prices and began posting a fixed, no-haggle price on every car. Its average profit per car sold rose by 8 percent compared with the year before. Previously, its salespeople had been free to cut prices during negotiations by whatever amount they judged necessary to close a sale. The dealership's owner concludes that customers are willing to pay more for the convenience of not having to haggle.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether Hartwell sold more cars in total last year than in the year before
Whether the prices Hartwell paid at wholesale auctions for the cars it sold were lower last year than the year before
Whether Hartwell's salespeople prefer selling cars at fixed prices
Whether some of Hartwell's customers last year had also bought cars from Hartwell before the switch
Whether no-haggle pricing is more common at new-car dealerships than at used-car dealerships
questions.explanation: Core move: profit per car depends on both selling price and cost, so the useful question is the one that tests whether the profit gain came from the customer side at all. If Hartwell's purchase costs fell, the higher profit could have come from cheaper inventory, not higher prices paid by customers, weakening the argument; if costs held steady, the gain must come from what customers paid, supporting it. The tempting trap is A, but the argument concerns profit per car, and total volume does not tell us whether each customer paid more. C concerns staff preferences, not customer behavior.

questions.stimulus: Last spring the Orrin Public Library extended its weekday closing time from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. Over the next six months, library card applications rose by 40 percent compared with the same months a year earlier. Admittedly, a large apartment complex near the library opened during that period, but applications from the complex's residents account for only a small share of the increase. The library's director concludes that the extended hours attracted many residents who previously had been unable to visit the library.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether residents of the new apartment complex tend to visit the library mainly in the evening
Whether the extended hours significantly raised the library's operating costs
Whether the library's evening visitors borrow more books per visit than its daytime visitors do
Whether the library had ever extended its hours on a previous occasion
Whether most of the additional card applications were submitted during the newly added evening hours
questions.explanation: Core move: find the question whose two possible answers point in opposite directions on the claimed mechanism. If most new applications came in after 6 p.m., the extended hours plausibly drew new users; if most came in during the old daytime hours, those applicants could have visited before, and the director's explanation weakens. The strongest trap is A, which revisits the concession, but the argument has already set the complex aside as accounting for only a small share, so its residents' habits cannot decide the issue. C sounds relevant because it compares evening and daytime visitors, but borrowing habits say nothing about who newly applied for cards.

questions.stimulus: Over the past three years, homes within two kilometers of the Kesby wind farm sold for 6 percent less, on average, than homes farther away in the same county. Opponents of a proposed second wind farm cite this as proof that turbines depress nearby home values. The Kesby farm's operator objects that the homes nearest the farm are, on average, older and smaller. Even so, the opponents are right: when nearby homes are compared only with farther homes of similar age and size, a gap of about 4 percent remains.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the argument?
choices: Whether residents living near the Kesby wind farm frequently complain about noise from its turbines
Whether the proposed second wind farm would be located closer to homes than the Kesby farm is
Whether, over the past three years, homes near the Kesby farm sold for less than homes of similar age and size farther away in the county
Whether, in the years before the Kesby farm was built, homes on the land near its site sold for less than similar homes elsewhere in the county
Whether homes near the Kesby farm are, on average, older and smaller than homes farther away
questions.explanation: Core move: the argument controls for age and size but never shows the gap appeared after the turbines arrived, so the key question is the pre-existing base rate. If nearby homes already sold for less before the farm existed, the 4 percent gap reflects something about the location and the argument collapses; if they sold at par, the turbines become the likely cause. The near-miss trap is C, which differs from D only in its time frame: the past three years fall after the farm was built, and the stimulus already answers that question with the 4 percent figure, so knowing it adds nothing. A only cuts one way (complaints would support the conclusion, but their absence would not undermine it, since turbines could depress prices for visual reasons), B bears on the proposed farm rather than this argument, and E is already conceded in the stimulus.

questions.stimulus: Every glaze stocked by the Harrowgate Pottery Cooperative has been certified food-safe. Marisol, a cooperative member, glazed her new set of soup bowls using only glazes she bought from the cooperative's stock. Marisol also owns several glazes that she bought from other suppliers, and at least one of those glazes has not been certified food-safe. She uses the glazes from other suppliers mainly on decorative tiles.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: None of the glazes Marisol bought from other suppliers has been certified food-safe.
Every certified food-safe glaze that Marisol owns was bought from the cooperative.
Marisol's new soup bowls were glazed only with glazes that have been certified food-safe.
Marisol has never applied an uncertified glaze to anything other than decorative tiles.
Some of the glazes stocked by the cooperative are unsuitable for decorative tiles.
questions.explanation: Core move: combine two facts directly. The bowls used only cooperative glazes, and every cooperative glaze is certified food-safe, so every glaze on the bowls is certified (C).
